text: Calculating moments of inertia. There are many applications for using the pre-computed moments of inertia in the figure, but there are instances where we need to calculate the moment of inertia for a shifted axis or for a compound object. Moment of inertia. We defined the moment of inertia i of an object as i equals some sub j, m sub j r sub j to the power of 2, for all the point masses that make up the object. Since r sub j measures the distance to the axis of rotation from each mass element m sub j, the moment of inertia for any object depends on the chosen axis. Consider two masses at the end of a massless or negligibly small mass, rod, and calculate the moment of inertia assuming two different rotation axes. Let's see the figure. In this case, the summation over the masses is simple because the two masses can be approximated as point masses, and the sum has only two terms. First, the axis is in the center of the barbell where each of the two masses m is a distance r away from the axis, a moment of inertia of i sub c equals some sub j, m sub j r sub j to the power of 2, equals m1 r1 to the power of 2, plus m2 r2 squared, equals mr squared, plus mr squared, equals 2mr squared. Second, the axis is at the end of the barbell, which gives a moment of inertia of i sub n, i sub e equals some sub j, m sub j, r to the power of 2, equals m sub 1 r1 squared, plus m sub 2 r2 squared, equals m0 squared, plus m2r squared, equals 4mr squared. From this result, we can conclude that it is twice as hard to rotate the barbell about the end, then about its center. Most objects are not point-like, so we need to think about each of the terms in the equation for the moment of inertia. The equation requires us to sum over each piece of mass m sub j that is a distance from the axis of rotation. Using our calculus knowledge, we break up the problems so that the piece of mass dm is infinitesimally small, see the figure. Then, we can write the moment of inertia by evaluating an integral over infinitesimal masses, rather than using a discrete sum over finite masses. i equals some sub j, m sub j, r sub j squared, therefore i equals integral r squared dm. In this form, we can generalize the calculation for moment of inertia to complex shapes. A uniform thin rod with axis in the middle. Consider a uniform in density and shape thin rod of mass m and length l, see the figure. We want a thin rod so that we can assume the cross-sectional area, i.e. circles at the ends of the rod, is small. Then, the rod can be approximated as a string of masses along a 1d straight line. The axis is perpendicular to the rod and passes through the midpoint for simplicity. We need to calculate the moment of inertia about the given axis. We orient the axis so that it aligns with the z axis and the x axis passes through the length of the rod. Then, we can integrate along the x axis. We define dm as a small mass element as a piece of the rod. The moment of inertia integral is an integral over the mass distribution. However, we need to integrate over space, not mass. Thus, we need to find a relationship between the mass and spatial variables. We do this using the linear mass density lambda of the object, which is the mass per unit length. Since the mass density of the object is uniform, we can spread the mass over the entire length, or lambda equals m over l, or m equals lambda l. If we take the differential of each side of this equation, i.e. breaking it into mass elements, we find dm equals d of lambda l equals lambda dl, since lambda is a constant. We can now see that our orientation of the rod along the x axis for convenience was a helpful choice. Note, a piece of rod dl lies completely along the x axis and has a length dx. In this situation, dl equals dx. We can therefore write dm equals lambda dx, which we know how to integrate. Using this all together, we have i equals integral r squared dm equals integral x squared dm equals integral x squared lambda dx. The rod extends from x equals negative l over 2 to x equals l over 2, since the axis lies in the middle of the rod at x equals 0. Then we have i equals integral sub-negative l over 2 to the power of l over 2, x squared lambda dx equals lambda over 3 x cubed, evaluated sub l over 2 to negative l over 2. Equals lambda over 3 times l over 2 cubed minus negative l over 2 cubed. Equals lambda over 3 times 2l cubed over 2 cubed equals lambda over 12l cubed. Since lambda equals m over l, we can substitute to find i equals 1 over 12 ml squared. We can compare to fig and see that our result matches the case for a thin rod about axis through center perpendicular to length. A uniform thin rod with axis at the end. Consider a uniform in density and shape, then rod of mass m and length l as before, but this time we move the axis of rotation to the end of the rod. See the figure. The only difference from before is the limits of integration, which is now from x equals 0 to x equals l. Thus, we can start from the integration step to get i equals integral sub-0 to the power of l, x squared lambda dx equals lambda over 3 x cubed, evaluated sub l to 0. Equals lambda over 3 times l cubed minus 0 cubed equals lambda over 3 l cubed equals 1 third ml squared. Note, the rotational inertia of the rod about its endpoint is larger than about its center by a factor of 4. This is consistent with the barbell example in the parallel axis theorem. The process between finding the moment of inertia of a rod using two different axes had mostly the same steps. This suggests that there might be a simpler method for determining the moment of inertia for a rod about any parallel axis through the center of mass. This is called the parallel axis theorem. Parallel axis theorem. Let m be the mass of an object, while d is the distance from an axis through the object's center of mass to a new axis. Then we have i parallel equals i c o m plus m d squared, where i parallel is the moment of inertia for the parallel axis, and i c o m is the moment of inertia through the center of mass. Let's use the case where the axis lies at the center of the rod, which is i c o m equals 1 over 12 ml squared. Then we can move the axis by a distance of l over 2 so that the axis now lies at the end of the rod. As a result, we find i parallel equals 1 over 12 ml squared plus m times l over 2 squared, equals 1 over 12 plus 1 over 4 ml squared equals 4 over 12 ml squared equals 1 over 3 ml squared. A uniform thin disk about an axis through its center. Integrating to find the moment of inertia for a 2D object is trickier, but one shape is commonly shown as a uniform thin disk about an axis through its center. Since the disk is thin, we can take the mass as distributed evenly across the entire x, y plane. Instead of a linear mass density, we have a relationship for the surface mass density or mass per unit surface area. The surface mass density sigma is constant for a thin disk, sigma equals m over a, therefore sigma a equals m, dm equals sigma dA. We apply a simplification for the area where it is composed of a series of thin rings. Each ring has a mass increment dm of radius r that is equidistant from the axis. The infinitesimal area of each ring is dA with a length 2 pi r times the infinitesimal width of each ring as dR. We can break the area of a circle into smaller pieces by a equals pi r squared, dA equals d pi r squared equals pi dr squared equals 2 pi r dr. The full disk area is then built by summing up all the thin rings with a radius range from r equals 0 to r equals r. This radius range becomes our limits of integration for dr. Putting this all together, we have i equals integral 0 to the power of r, r squared sigma dA equals integral 0 to the power of r, r squared sigma 2 pi r dr. Equals 2 pi sigma integral 0 to the power of r, r cubed dr equals pi sigma over 2 r to the power of 4, evaluated from 0 to the power of r, equals pi over 2 sigma r to the power of 4. Then we can substitute sigma equals m over a, and for a disk we have sigma equals m over pi r squared. Thus we obtain i equals pi over 2 times m over pi r squared times r to the fourth equals 1 over 2 m r squared. This result matches the standard moment of inertia for a uniform solid disk about an axis through its center, calculating the moment of inertia for compound objects. Consider a compound object with a disk on the end of a rod, see the figure. This object is not uniformly shaped, so the integration is not so easy. However, if we use the definition for the moment of inertia as a summation, we can reason that a compound object's moment of inertia can be determined as the sum of each part of the object. i sub-tote equals sum sub j i sub j. Note, the moments of inertia must share a common axis. In the above example, this would be a rod of length L rotating about its end, and a thin disk of radius r rotating about an axis shifted off center by a distance L plus r, where r is the radius of the disk. The mass of the rod is m sub r, while the mass of the disk is m sub d. We already know the moment of inertia for the rod as 1 third m sub r L squared, but we have to use the parallel axis theorem to find the moment of inertia for the disk about the given axis. The moment of inertia of the disk about its center of mass is 1 over 2 meters sub d r to the power of 2. Now, we can apply the parallel axis theorem to get i parallel equals i c o m plus m d squared equals 1 over 2 meters sub d r to the power of 2 plus m sub d times L plus r squared. Adding the moment of inertia of the rod to the moment of inertia of the disk with a shifted axis of rotation, we find the moment of inertia for the compound object is i total equals 1 over 3 meters sub r L to the power of 2 plus 1 over 2 meters sub d r to the power of 2 plus m sub d times L plus r squared. Note, we could expand the above result to collect terms in meters sub d r to the power of 2. However, the overall number of terms would be larger. There would be an additional meters sub d L squared plus 2 meters sub d L r from expanding the square, resulting in 4 terms which does not really make it any simpler. Example problem, person on a merry go round. The problem, a 25 kilogram child stands at a distance r equals 1.0 meters from the axis of a rotating merry go round. The merry go round can be approximated as a uniform solid disk with a mass of 500 kilograms and a radius of 2.0 meters. Find the moment of inertia of this system. The worked solution follows. The model. The system consists of two parts, the child and the merry go round. The child is modeled as a point mass located 1.0 meters from the axis and the merry go round is modeled as a uniform solid disk rotating about its center. The total moment of inertia of the system is the sum of the moment of inertia of the child and the moment of inertia of the disk. The math. The moment of inertia of the child is given by the point mass expression i sub c equals m r squared. The child's moment of inertia follows from the point mass expression i sub c equals 25 kilograms times 1.0 meters squared. equals 25 kilograms dot square meters. The moment of inertia of the merry go round is given by the uniform disk expression i sub m equals 1 over 2 capital m r squared. The merry go round's moment of inertia follows from the uniform disk expression i sub m equals 1 over 2 times 500 kilograms times 2.0 meters squared equals 1,000 kilograms dot square meters. The total moment of inertia of the system is the sum of these two contributions. i total equals i sub c plus i sub m equals 25 kilograms dot square meters plus 1,000 kilograms dot square meters equals 1,025 kilograms dot square meters is approximately equal to 1,000 kilograms dot square meters. The conclusion. The moment of inertia of the child merry go round system is 1,000 kilograms dot square meters. This result shows that the total moment of inertia is dominated by the merry go round rather than the child. The disk contributes much more because it has far more mass distributed over a larger radius. Example problem, rod and solid sphere. The problem. Find the moment of inertia of the rod and solid sphere combination about the two axes as shown below. The rod has length 0.5 meters and mass 2.0 kilograms. The radius of the sphere is 20 centimeters and the sphere has mass 1 kilogram. For part a, find the moment of inertia about the axis through point a at the top of the rod. For part b, find the moment of inertia about the axis through point a at the junction of the rod and the sphere. The worked solution follows. The model. The object is a compound system consisting of a slender rod and a solid sphere. The total moment of inertia about either axis is the sum of the moment of inertia of the rod and the moment of inertia of the sphere about that same axis. The rod rotates about an axis through one end so its contribution is found using the standard result for a thin rod about one end. The sphere rotates about an axis that does not pass through its center so its contribution is found using the parallel axis theorem. The distance from the sphere's center to the rotation axis depends on which of the two axes is chosen. The math. The total moment of inertia is the sum of the rod and sphere contributions. I total equals I rod plus I sphere. The rod rotates about an axis through one end so its moment of inertia is I rod equals 1 over 3 m rod l squared. equals 1 over 3 times 2.0 kilograms times 0.5 meters squared. equals 0.17 kilograms dot square meters. The sphere is a solid sphere so its moment of inertia about its center of mass is I cm equals 2 over 5 m sphere times r squared. I cm equals 2 over 5 times 1.0 kilograms times 0.20 meters squared equals 0.016 kilograms dot square meters. For part A the axis is at the top of the rod. The center of the sphere is therefore a distance l plus r from the axis. The parallel axis theorem gives I sphere equals I cm plus m sphere times l plus r squared. equals 0.016 kilograms dot square meters plus 1.0 kilograms times 0.50 meters plus 0.20 meters squared. equals 0.016 kilograms dot square meters plus 0.49 kilograms dot square meters equals 0.51 kilograms dot square meters. The total moment of inertia is therefore I total equals 0.17 kilograms dot square meters plus 0.51 kilograms dot square meters equals 0.68 kilograms dot square meters. For part B the axis is at the junction of the rod and the sphere. The center of the sphere is therefore a distance r from the axis. The parallel axis theorem gives I sphere equals I cm plus m sphere times r squared equals 0.016 kilograms dot square meters plus 1.0 kilograms times 0.20 meters squared. equals 0.016 kilograms dot square meters plus 0.040 kilograms dot square meters equals 0.056 kilograms dot square meters. The total moment of inertia is therefore I total equals 0.17 kilograms dot square meters plus 0.51 kilograms dot square meters equals 0.68 kilograms dot square meters. The conclusion. The moment of inertia of the rod sphere system is 0.68 kilograms dot square meters about the axis through the top of the rod and it is 0.23 kilograms dot square meters about the axis through the junction of the rod and sphere. These results show that the moment of inertia is larger when the axis is farther from the mass of the sphere. Moving the axis closer to the center of mass of the system reduces the resistance to rotational acceleration. Example problem. Angular velocity of a pendulum. The problem. A pendulum in the shape of a rod figure here is released from rest at an angle of 30 degrees. It has a length 30 centimeters and mass 300 grams. What is its angular velocity at its lowest point? The worked solution follows. The model. The pendulum is modeled as a uniform rod rotating about one end because it is released from rest and air resistance is neglected. The mechanical energy of the system is conserved during the motion. As the rod swings downward, the loss in gravitational potential energy of its center of mass is converted into rotational kinetic energy. The center of mass of a uniform rod is located at its midpoint and the moment of inertia of a uniform rod about one end is used to relate the rotational kinetic energy to the angular velocity. The math. The rod has length L equals 30 centimeters equals 0.30 meters. The center of mass of a uniform rod is located at a distance L over 2 from the pivot. When the rod is released from an angle theta, the vertical drop of the center of mass between the release point and the lowest point is delta H equals L over 2 times 1 minus cosine theta. The loss in gravitational potential energy is therefore C exercise 8.7 delta U equals MGL over 2 times 1 minus cosine theta. At the lowest point, the rod has rotational kinetic energy via K equals 1 over 2 I omega to the power of 2. Conservation of mechanical energy requires that the loss in gravitational potential energy equals the gain in rotational kinetic energy, which gives MGL over 2 times 1 minus cosine theta equals 1 over 2 times 1 third ML squared omega to the power of 2. We must now solve for the angular velocity, which gives omega equals square root of 3G over L times 1 minus cosine theta. The angular velocity follows from the energy expression with G equals 9.81 meter per second squared, L equals 0.30 meters and theta equals 30 degrees. Omega equals square root of 3 times 9.81 meter per second squared over 0.30 meters times 1 minus cosine 30 degrees equals 3.6 radians per second. The conclusion, the angular velocity of the rod at its lowest point is 3.6 radians per second. This result shows that the angular speed depends on the geometry of the rod and the release angle, but not on the mass of the rod. In this idealized model, the mass cancels because both the gravitational potential energy and the rotational kinetic energy are proportional to the mass.
